## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. ## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll stay at 20k for game 17. As Black, I’ll count area early, secure eye boundaries before the board closes, and save the full record and review for the next session.

# Game 15: Black vs 20k — W+8

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 66–67: 67 moves, 65 stone moves.
Final captures: Black 7, White 3. No invalid move, ko or resignation occurred.
The final scoring board matched the last playing board; no dead-stone removal was needed.

The 20k record is now three wins and eight losses. Retain 20k. The lower group survived and repelled two invasions, but scored only forty area. The three-stone top entry died.

## Records and verified score

- game-015.sgf contains all 67 moves.
- game-015-log.json contains all 34 play responses with full returned positions, current-board groups/liberties/empty regions, the complete move list, counting notes and corrections. Opponent selection is recorded as confirmed metadata.
- Official result: W+8.
- Independent count: Black 30 stones + 10 territory = 40; White 25 stones + 16 territory = 41, plus seven komi = 48. No neutral points.
- Black area by rows 1–9: 9, 9, 8, 7, 5, 2, 0, 0, 0.
- White area by rows 1–9: 0, 0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 9, 9.
- Black territory: A3/B3, B1, D1/D2/E1, D4, F2/G2, J1.
- White territory: A8/A9/B9/C8/C9/D9, E8/F7/F8, G9, H7/H8/J7/J8/J9, J5.

## Opening and early count: a lower framework without a winning margin

1 B C3, 2 W G7, 3 B G3, 4 W C7,
5 B C5, 6 W C6, 7 B D5, 8 W E6,
9 B E5, 10 W F5, 11 B F4, 12 W G5,
13 B G4, 14 W H5.

The first count, after move 8, treated the entire lower five rows as an explicitly unsecured 45-point target. That would only give the minimum Black winning split. No current group was called alive or territory secure.

After move 14, the revised outline was only 41: rows 1–4 all nine each (36), plus A–E in row 5 (five). White F5/G5/H5 occupied the rest of that boundary, and J5 was excluded. This count correctly showed the need for more space.

15 B D6, 16 W D7,
17 B B6, 18 W B7, 19 B B5, 20 W A6,
21 B A5, 22 W A7,
23 B E4, 24 W H4,
25 B H3, 26 W J3,
27 B J2, 28 W J4, 29 B H2, 30 W F6,
31 B C4, 32 W E7.

D6 and B6 added two retained points in row 6. B5 immediately connected the two-liberty B6 stone to C5; A5 prevented the left undercut and White A7 connected A6 upward. E4 joined the C5/D5/E5 chain to F4/G4/G3. H3 blocked the right descent; J2 put J3 in atari, White J4 connected upward, and H2 promptly joined J2 to the main group. C4 connected C3.

However, White H4/J4/J3 removed three points from the earlier lower outline. After move 32 it was 40:
- Rows 1–2: nine each = 18.
- Row 3: eight, excluding White J3.
- Row 4: seven, A–G.
- Row 5: five, A–E.
- Row 6: B6/D6, two.
Total 40, still provisional until the later invasions were settled.

The eventual score did not arise from losing the lower group. This framework itself was too small. With 40 against 41 plus komi, shifting four White points to Black would only draw; shifting five would win B+2. Development around moves 9–15 needed to contest more than the two retained row-6 points, or establish a second viable base earlier. No single opening replacement is verified. E5/D6 were not shown individually wrong, and this opening is not established as losing against every reply.

## Top entry: eye hopes were blocked, then a diagonal liberty was imagined

33 B F8, 34 W G8,
35 B E8, 36 W D8,
37 B F7, 38 W F9,
39 B H1, 40 W E9 captured E8/F7/F8.

Before F8, prospective E9/G9 eyes were named, requiring D9/F9/H9 and E8/G8 boundaries. These were needed future stones, not secure eyes. White G8 immediately denied the proposed right boundary. E8 tried to expand left, but White D8 closed that side. After move 36 the two-stone group had exactly E9/F7/F9.

The decisive reading mistake was F7. The session imagined it might add a G6 escape route and attack the separated White chains. But F7's orthogonal neighbors are E7, G7, F6 and F8. G6 is diagonal. E7/G7/F6 were all White; F8 was already Black. F7 added NO liberty and reduced the group to E9/F9. White F9 then left only E9.

This is more concrete than a general life-planning failure: the current inventory contradicted the imagined extension. Before playing an escape move, list its actual empty orthogonal neighbors and check that at least one route is added. F7 was not forcing and could have been omitted.

Manual reading after move 38:
- B E9 has only D9 for the entire four-stone group; W D9 captures all four immediately.
- Alternatively B E9, W G9, B D9 adds C9 as the only liberty; W C9 captures five.
These lines do not prove every earlier F8 replacement fails. They establish that the chosen continuation had no demonstrated rescue and that extending along the first line would add doomed stones against the stated replies.

The in-game log initially included an invalid branch after B E9/W D9, imagining Black could next capture F9 with G9. That ignored White D9's immediate four-stone capture and the liberties it opens. A final correction explicitly discards that branch. Do not inherit it as a valid variation.

Black abandoned the three stones, and actual White E9 captured them. None belonged to the forty-point lower outline, which survived unchanged. F8/E8/F7 is not a living invasion pattern; no single saving top-entry replacement is verified.

## Lower life: one efficient connecting move supplied the second eye

39 B H1 connected to H2 and secured J1, bordered by H1/J2.
41 B D3 connected through C3 and secured D4, bordered by C4/D3/D5/E4.

All boundaries were in one connected Black group. White at either eye would capture nothing and be suicide because Black retained the other. The lower group was unconditionally alive before the invasion cleanup. An earlier idea of building a G2 eye through F2/G1 would have needed more moves; D3 completed an existing eye boundary directly.

Preserve this habit: inspect already surrounded empty points and identify the missing boundary connection before constructing an entirely new eye. D3 here is a position-specific life move, not a generic opening recommendation.

## Lower-left invasion: deny both escape boundaries before the corner develops

42 W B2, 43 B C2, 44 W B1,
45 B C1, 46 W B3,
47 B B4, 48 W A3, 49 B A4.

C2/C1 blocked right and bottom escape while connected to the living main group. B4 stopped the upward route; A4 joined A5/B4 and closed the remaining first-line boundary. The White A3/B1/B2/B3 group then had exactly A1/A2, one two-point space.

61 B A2, 62 W H9,
63 B A1 captured four, 64 W B8,
65 B B2 connected A1/A2 to C2.

Before A1, both Black A2 and White's four stones had only A1. Black A1 captured the enemy first and opened A3/B1/B2. White A1 instead would have captured Black A2, but left five White stones only A2; Black A2 would then capture five. This is neither seki nor ko.

B2 promptly connected the capturing corner stones to the already living main group. The four captures restored points within the existing outline; they did not expand Black's forty-point boundary.

## Lower-center invasion: block the outside liberty, capture, reconnect

50 W E3, 51 B E2, 52 W F2,
53 B F3 captured E3, 54 W G2,
55 B G1, 56 W G6,
57 B F1 captured F2/G2, 58 W H6,
59 B E3 connected E2, 60 W J6.

White E3 initially had only E2/F3. Black E2 denied the lower escape; its own liberties were D2/E1, then E3 after the capture. White F2 did not save E3. Black F3 joined F4/G3 while capturing it, reopening E3 for adjacent groups.

White F2/G2 then had F1/G1. Black G1 connected through H1 and left them only F1. White G6 ignored the atari; Black F1 captured both and joined G1. White F1 instead would have extended to three stones with only E1; Black E1 could capture all three. The played captures were verified for actual replies; they do not validate an opening as forced.

Black E3 then joined the isolated E2 stone to D3/E4/F3. The capture and reconnection left F2/G2 as a separate two-point eye space, with connected Black boundaries E2/F1/F3/G1/G3/H2. D4/J1 remained intact throughout.

## Passing and carry forward

66 W pass, 67 B pass.
Before passing, every Black stone was connected, the two invasions had been physically removed, and the independent 40–41 area count predicted W+8 exactly.

1. Retain 20k: three wins and eight losses. Reliable current-board inventories and surviving groups have not yet produced consistent sufficient area.
2. Act on a deficit earlier. The move-14 outline was 41; D6/B6 gains and right reductions left 40 by move 32. A late unsupported top entry did not repair it.
3. An extension must add an orthogonal liberty. F7 was diagonal to G6 and added none. Compare the imagined route to the actual inventory BEFORE playing.
4. Treat prospective eyes as conditional on specific boundary turns. G8/D8 denied the F8 plan promptly; E9/F9 was one connected edge space.
5. Keep the successful lower habits: B6–B5, E4, J2–H2, C4, D3, E2–E3 and corner B2 connections; preserve true D4/J1 eyes during cleanup.
6. Remove enclosed invasions and connect the capturing stones. This protected forty area, but did not create the five-point territorial shift needed to win.

All move choices and tactical variations were manual. Code only parsed returned current boards, counted current stones/groups/liberties/empty regions and final area, kept records, and converted moves to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.

# Game 16: White vs 20k — Draw

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 50–51. There were 51 moves: 48 stone moves and three passes (Black 31, White 50, Black 51).
Final captures: Black 0, White 0. No ko, invalid move or resignation occurred.

## Records and independent score

- game-016-log.json contains opponent selection, all 25 play responses, all 26 returned positions, current-board group/liberty/empty-region inventories, complete moves, counting notes and corrections, and the independent final count.

- The final displayed board still contains White F6/G5/G6/H4/H5. These five stones were never physically captured. The independent count manually excludes them as dead; the resulting score agrees with the official draw. Do not report five captures or a visibly changed scoring board.

## Left development: connection worked; the outline had little room

Opening:
1 B E5, 2 W C3, 3 B G7, 4 W C7, 5 B G3,
6 W D5, 7 B D7, 8 W C6, 9 B D4,
10 W D6, 11 B E6.

C3/C7 supplied two left footholds. D5 contested the central boundary, but after D4 it had only C5/D6. D6 promptly joined D5 to C6/C7. This was an actual orthogonal connection, not a diagonal assumption.

The first explicitly unsecured outline, before move 10, was A–C in all rows (27) plus D5/D6 (2, including the intended D6): 29. No secure territory or unconditional life was claimed.

12 W D8 put isolated D7 in atari at E7 while extending the top.
13 B E7 joined D7 to E5/E6.
14 W C8 directly joined D8 to C7.
15 B E8 stopped further expansion along row 8.

At move 15, A–C all rows plus D5/D6/D8 gave 30 provisional points. The in-game note first repeated 29, then corrected it to 30 in the same note. E8 was Black; it was not included. The left outline plainly needed lower expansion or another viable region.

16 W D3, 17 B E4,
18 W E3, 19 B F3,
20 W F2, 21 B G2,
22 W E2, 23 B G1.

D3/E3 joined C3 and extended while lower routes were still open. F2 was initially disconnected from E3; after G2 it had exactly E2/F1. E2 immediately joined it to E3. The actual played replies allowed this connection. No proof is claimed that Black's alternative cut at E2 fails.

The revised unsecured outline was 38:
A–C all rows = 27;
D5/D6/D8 = 3;
D1–D3/E1–E3/F1–F2 = 8.
That was the minimum White winning total with all points assigned, leaving no margin for reductions.

24 W C4 protected against a D4 incursion.
25 B F1, 26 W E1,
27 B D9, 28 W C9, 29 B E9,
30 W C5, 31 B pass.

C4 joined the lower chain. C9 blocked the upper undercut and put D9 in atari; E9 connected D9 to Black's main chain. C5 then joined both White groups through C4/C6/D5. Every left stone survived.

F1 reduced the outline from 38 to 37; D9 denied a hoped-for additional top point. The resulting left region was enough for a draw, not a win. Considering F1 instead of C4 at move 24 is an unverified hypothesis: Black could then enter C4, so preserving F1 alone is not a demonstrated net gain or winning replacement. Earlier development around moves 10–16 also deserves reconsideration. No individual opening move is established as best or losing.

## Essential correction: Black F1 connected through G1

Before White C4, the in-game reading incorrectly claimed that Black F1 would be isolated with only E1, so White E1 would capture it.

This was wrong. Black had already played G1 at move 23. F1 is orthogonally adjacent to G1, and Black F1 joined F3/G1/G2/G3 through G1. The returned group inventory after move 25 explicitly showed all five connected Black stones with several liberties.

White E1 blocked the further undercut and connected through E2; it captured nothing. The mistake was corrected before E1, and no later move relied on the imagined capture.

Carry forward a concrete check: before calling a new enemy stone an atari, list ALL its orthogonal neighbors and identify every same-color group it joins. Counting only the local empty E1 missed the existing G1 connection. A current-board inventory helps only when the manual reading respects it.

## Right invasion: open space did not guarantee enough boundary turns

After Black's first pass, White tried to improve on the 37-point draw:
32 W G5, 33 B F4,
34 W H5, 35 B H6,
36 W H4, 37 B H3,
38 W G6, 39 B H7,
40 W F6, 41 B F7.

G5 began in a broad open region, with F5/G4/G6/H5 available. Prospective eyes were named, including H5 with G5/H4/H6/J5 boundaries and J7 with H7/J6/J8 boundaries. All required future boundary turns; none was secure.

H5 expanded right, but Black H6 denied the proposed upper boundary. H4 tried to develop downward; Black H3 denied the lower endpoint. The alternative prospective J4/J6 eyes also depended on boundaries that Black occupied. G6 then used a real central route through F6. F6's only new liberty was F7 (F5 was already a group liberty); Black F7 immediately closed it and connected G7/H6/H7 to the main Black group.

After move 41 the five White stones had only F5/G4/J4/J5. F5 and G4 were bordered on their other sides by connected Black stones. J4/J5 were one edge route with Black H3/H6 outside boundaries, not two eyes. The central extension did not reach a viable base.

White abandoned these five stones at move 42 instead of adding stones to the closed strip. Black later played G8/J3/J5/J4. At the finish, the right group had exactly F5/G4:
- W F5 adds no liberty and leaves all six stones only G4; B G4 captures six.
- W G4 adds no liberty and leaves all six stones only F5; B F5 captures six.
- B F5 leaves the existing five White stones only G4; W G4 is suicide because Black F5 joins the large living Black group and captures nothing. Black can then capture at G4.
Neither space is a White eye. There is no ko or seki.

The failed G5/H5/H4/G6/F6 continuation is not a living pattern. The draw does not validate it. Reconsider the invasion's entry, timing and minimum boundary turns before Black H6/H3 close both directions. No single rescue or earlier replacement was verified.

## Finish two true eyes before passing

42 W C2, 43 B G8,
44 W D1, 45 B J3,
46 W B2, 47 B J5,
48 W B1, 49 B J4,
50 W pass, 51 B pass.

C2/D1 completed true D2, bounded by White C2/D1/D3/E2.
B2 joined C2, then B1 joined B2 and completed true C1, bounded by White B1/C2/D1.
Every boundary belonged to the one connected nineteen-stone White main group. At either eye, Black would capture nothing because White retained the other eye, so either attempted fill is suicide. The broad remaining left territory was additional space; it was not used as a substitute for this explicit proof.

The final left region retained the entire 37-point outline. White passed knowing that the right stones were dead and that 37+7 versus 44 should draw. The official result matched that count.

## Carry forward

1. Retain 20k: three wins, eight losses, one draw. Preserve the main-group connection and counting habits.
2. Scan every orthogonal same-color neighbor before declaring an enemy stone in atari. F1 joined G1; E1 never captured it.
3. A minimum winning outline needs a margin. The provisional 38 lost F1 and became a draw. Contest sufficient territory before relying on another invasion.
4. Name the boundary turns and compare them with the opponent's simplest enclosure. The right had open liberties initially, but H6/H3 and then F7 denied both eyes and escape.
5. Keep the exact left life proof: C2/D1 for D2, then B2/B1 for C1, with all boundaries connected. Stop adding stones to a group once its extensions create no new route or eye.

Goal: improve at 9x9 Go across fresh sessions, ultimately win consistently against human-style KataGo 9d.

- Game 1: Black vs 9d, Chinese area scoring, komi 7. Lost by resignation after White move 56 (D2).
- Game 2: White vs 4k, same rules. Lost by resignation after Black move 49 (J6). No captures or numerical final score.

- Game 9: Black vs 20k, same rules. Lost W+42 after consecutive passes at moves 67–68. Area: Black 23, White 58 plus 7 komi. - Read game-014.md for the review; game-014.sgf and game-014-log.json contain all 61 stone moves, all 31 distinct returned positions plus resignation, current-board inventories and early counting notes. Its lower-left dead-group and upper F9/G9 proofs are manual; no final numerical score or official dead-stone adjudication occurred.
- Read game-015.md for its review; game-015.sgf and game-015-log.json contain all 67 moves (65 stone moves, two passes), all 34 play responses with current-board inventories, early counts, a corrected diagonal-liberty mistake and invalid hypothetical capture branch, and verified final area.
- Read game-016.md for the latest review; game-016.sgf and game-016-log.json contain all 51 moves (48 stone moves, three passes), all 26 returned positions with inventories, early counts, the corrected F1/G1 connection mistake, explicit C1/D2 life proof and independent 44–37 area count after marking the five dead right stones.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
22. Check where an atari extension ends before making the contact move. Game 6's B6 was left with only A6 by Black B7; White A6 would leave two stones with only A7, allowing Black A7 to capture both. White B8 secured the upper wall but Black A6 captured B6.
23. Repair vulnerable connections before tenuki. In game 7, F9 had only F8/G9 and was disconnected from E8. Black G2 allowed White F8/G8 to trap the top stones. F8 before tenuki is an unverified candidate connecting F9 to E8, not an established winning move.
24. A counter-atari may release the opponent when they capture first. After game 7's Black F7 at move 47, White F8/G8 had only H8, but Black F9/G9 had only H9. White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.
25. A diagonal framework also needs a concrete area count. Game 7's vague estimate of about 45 was unsupported; the later row count gave only 38 potential points even with the top intact. Losing seven top points left 31. The main group did live: G6 (F6/G5/G7/H6 boundaries) and J6 (H6/J5/J7 boundaries) were independent true eyes after H7 connected all boundaries.
26. Empty prospective eye points need secured boundaries and enough turns. Game 7's G2 invasion lost its right route to White H2 and its left route to White F2. Then Black G1, White F1, Black H1, White J1 would capture three. Black abandoned G2 instead; White G1 captured it. Do not treat the G2 entry as a proven living pattern.
27. Three corner approaches are not three living bases. In game 8, White C7/C3/G7/E7 built a surviving top wall, but C3 was left alone until move 22. After Black A3, the lower-left had only E4/D3/B2/B1. C1 protected the right first-line boundary but did not preserve the left boundary. Black E2 connected E3 to D2/D1; White E4, Black F4 closed the last central route, leaving only B2/B1. Black A2/B1/B2 captured eight. Develop a second base before the wall and undercuts close it; no saving replacement is verified.
28. An extension into one temporary liberty is not an escape. In game 8, White E4 added F4, which Black immediately occupied. The corner could not save the group: after move 35, W B2, B A2, W B1, B A1 captures ten. Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves only A1; W A1 is legal but leaves only A2, where Black connects B2 to A3 and captures ten. Do not confuse this legal one-liberty extension with suicide.
29. An edge strip also needs an outside boundary. Game 8's H3/H2/H1 had only J3/J2/J1 after Black H4/G2/G1. J4 was unsecured, so these were not two eyes. Black J3/J2/J1 captured all three; White J1 was suicide because Black J2/J3 retained J4. Do not reuse this late entry as a living pattern.
30. Game 8's top main group had true eyes D7 (C7/D6/E7/D8) and E9 (D9/E8/F9), all boundaries connected White. B7/C8/C9 then contained A7/B8; A8 and B9 captured them. H8/G9/J9 captured H9. Rebuilding liberties after captures preserved the top, but its 33 area still lost to 48 plus the komi adjustment. Life and sufficient area remain separate tests.

31. Game 9's capture of White A4/A5 at move 45 left Black only A4/A5: one two-point eye. Black A1 later captured A2, but A1 itself had only A2. 59 B B5, 60 W B6,
61 B A6 captured A3/A4/A5, 62 W A7,

75 B D4, 76 W G1,
77 B J1 captured G1/H1, 78 W H1 captured J1,
79 B G1, 80 W B8,
81 B J1 captured H1, 82 W C9,
83 B H1 connected J1, 84 W A9,

The final lower group had 25 stones and five territory points = 30; the upper group had 16 stones and two eyes = 18. No major Black group died. White captured only the two isolated J1 stones during the right-corner exchanges.

White's final stones were several disconnected groups, but each retained at least two separate shared eye liberties. Thus their disconnected appearance did not imply dead stones.

1. Retain 20k: four wins, eight losses, one draw. One win after a draw is not consistent strength.

4. Count contested points separately. D4/G1 mattered before passing; final 30 + 18 = 48 matched B+8.
5. Distinguish a two-stone capture from a one-stone ko. The J1/H1 exchanges changed character only after G1 became Black.
6. The three left captures and central F6 capture relied on ignored ataris. Preserve the tactical habits without claiming they will recur against stronger opponents.

All moves and variations were manual. Code only inspected current returned positions, counted groups/liberties/area, kept records and converted moves to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.
`;

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.

Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
